title: Branch-resolved Pauli-block spectroscopy of residual conditional phase in two-qubit gates
authors: Xudan Chai, Yanwu Gu, Huiqi Xue, Kerui Li, Dong E. Liu
abstract: Recent progress in quantum physics and quantum technologies is driving quantum computing from the noisy intermediate-scale (NISQ) era toward fault-tolerant operation. High-precision control of two-qubit gates is among the most critical requirements in this transition and hinges on accurate two-qubit calibration. For controlled-phase and CZ-style operations, the residual conditional phase (the nonlocal ZZ-type deviation after local compensation) is weakly resolved at leading order in average infidelity and randomized benchmarking, and repeated Ramsey amplification does not reliably isolate it from ordinary target detuning, SPAM errors, and contrast loss in long sequences. We introduce branch-resolved Pauli-block spectroscopy to estimate the per-cycle residual ZZ-rotation angle theta_c with its sign, from which the controlled-phase residual follows by a fixed convention. The protocol repeats a fixed probe for N cycles, measures the closed Pauli block IX, IY, ZX, and ZY, and forms branch coherences C+ and C- conditioned on the control qubit; theta_c splits the two branch phase slopes in opposite directions, while local target phase beta_c shifts them together. An echoed-cycle variant suppresses removable local terms while preserving the nonlocal contribution. Numerical simulations with injected theta_c, detuning, damping, and SPAM confirm unbiased signed readout where scalar-sector alternatives fail and distinguish opposite-sign errors at equal infidelity. On one superconducting cloud qubit-coupler pair, a pulse-level calibration closed loop shows near-linear injection, preserved branch contrast, and tracking of the native residual conditional phase through one iteration. The approach yields a low-overhead, signed per-cycle estimate of residual conditional phase that standard fidelity benchmarks underresolve at leading order.
summary: The paper introduces branch-resolved Pauli-block spectroscopy to overcome limitations in calibrating residual conditional phases ($\vartheta_c$) in two-qubit gates. By measuring specific coherences derived from a closed Pauli block, the technique extracts a signed estimate of $\vartheta_c$, which is crucial because standard fidelity measurements are sign-blind. This method was successfully demonstrated on superconducting qubits, providing a low-overhead tool for active quantum control.
main_problem: Accurately calibrating the residual conditional phase ($\vartheta_c$) in two-qubit gates is critical for advancing quantum computation beyond the NISQ era.
main_result: The authors developed a branch-resolved spectroscopy technique that yields a signed, per-cycle estimate of $\vartheta_c$, which standard fidelity benchmarks fail to resolve or distinguish from noise.
method: They employ Pauli-block spectroscopy by measuring specific coherences ($C_\pm$) derived from the closed Pauli block $\{IX, IY, ZX, ZY\}$ and fitting the resulting phase slopes to extract $\vartheta_c$.
model_or_system: The work is implemented on a superconducting cloud qubit-coupler pair, focusing on controlled-phase or CZ-style two-qubit gates. The dynamics are analyzed by tracking the evolution of Pauli moments.
key_observables: Signed per-cycle residual ZZ-rotation angle ($\vartheta_c$), branch coherences ($C_\pm$), and gate fidelity ($F_{avg}$).
important_parameters: The measurement is sensitive to $\vartheta_c$ (the target), the local detuning phase ($ eta_c$), contrast decay ($\Gamma$), and noise sources like SPAM.
main_assumptions: The method relies on reconstructing the closed Pauli block $\{IX, IY, ZX, ZY\}$ and assumes that the differential measurement of branch coherences can separate $\vartheta_c$ from common-mode local errors ($ eta_c$).
figures_summary: Figures compare the sign-blind average gate infidelity against the signed estimate derived from branch readout, demonstrating the superior sensitivity of the proposed method.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical problem (calibration difficulty), details the theoretical framework using Pauli expansion and defining branch coherences ($C_\pm$), presents the fitting procedure to extract $\vartheta_c$, validates this approach via numerical simulations under noise, and concludes with experimental demonstration on superconducting qubits showing successful closed-loop calibration.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, high-precision metrology tool for characterizing fundamental gate errors in solid-state quantum hardware, directly addressing the primary bottleneck for fault-tolerant computation.
